doc.title: Spiegle Willcox and Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Norwich, New York, November 14, 1995

title: Gallodoro's cassette of solos and his meagre royalties
summary: Gallodoro describes a compilation of his recordings from 1944 to 1951, his tonguing, and the tiny royalties on Fantasy Impromptu and the Brahms Clarinet Quartet.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Well we look forward to many more years of hearing you guys, and we have some instruments here, which is a real treat.
Can I just say something about my—

My cassette here, what I did, I compiled sixteen solos, my whole Columbia album that I recorded in 1951, then I have live performances that I did at ABC in 1947 like “Dizzy Fingers,” 1944 “Flight of the Bumble Bee” on clarinet, and some I did in McAllen Texas, then it shows double and triple tonguing, which I’m one of the very few that does it. My brother says, “Al, when you double or triple tongue it sounds like single tongue.” That’s because I trained myself correctly to do it. So anyway, there’s a lot of good stuff in here.
So this is like a career compilation for you. That’s great.

Then I do the “Fantasy Impromptu,” which was published by Mel’s Music. You know how much money I made on that? Royalties? Is there any price on peanut shells? Three dollars royalty. A dollar and a half. Terrible.
Well the business of music can sometimes be a little treacherous. But there’s not that many saxophonists or reed players that can step from the classical world into the jazz/popular music.

That’s because I’ve been all around playing. And this proves it. This proves, now I do one number here that I recorded on the Columbia album. “Alte Wien” Old Vienna that I do with strings, harp and alto sax. That’s real classical, you know. It’s a different thing. This is a variety of all my playing, except the heavy, like Brahms. I recorded the Brahms Clarinet Quartet with the Stuyvesant Quartet in New York in 1947. There again, we didn’t get one penny royalty. Not one penny royalty. It was International Records, then they put it on Concert Hall Recording and that was it.
